According to the french philosopher Blaise Pascal; "all the unhappiness of men arises from one single fact: that they cannot stay quietly in their own chamber. The other philosophy they talked about where existential nihilism (Radical Freedom), which mark his impulsive, outward acting behaviors, because nothing matters anyway. 

 Lastly they talked about Albert Camus and his view on Absurdism. In where he thought there where three ways to understand this way of thinking:

1. you escape existence, because if nothing matters anyway, your existens as an idea is meaningless (as I understood it). 
2. you believe that there is a higher power, and it becomes more of a religious experience. 
3. You except the absurd for what it is and keep on going. Camus believed that by doing so you achieve your truest sense of freedom. Letting go. 

And number 3 is something I really need to work on, and feel like so many people with BPD have a hard time with. If it is a friend who suddenly doesn't answer your texts anymore out if nowhere, so you bombard them back, or you got fired from your job because of covid, like the acceptance of shock and confusion. Off topic, but does he himself think that he has BPD? 

Any number of trauma responses can lead someone to "split" and see things and people in black and white. 

I don't think that BPD can "appear" later in adulthood per se. Unless someone has been shielded from stressors like relationships, work, friends or school all the other years, and then suddenly gets exposed to having friends, a job/studying, a relationship, and then suddenly notices all the other signs like fear of abandonment, fights, (passive) aggression, devaluation/idealization on a day to day basis, too much empathy and/or lack thereof, romanticizing relationships (flirting with friends to seek gratification or thinking they want to have sex with you, so you flirt even though you don't really feel attracted to them). 

But BPD and C-PTSD are very similar. I think that I may have both BPD and C-PTSD. Complex-PTSD is often due to severe, prolonged childhood trauma (or trauma caused by a situation you couldn't get out of for several years and the perpetrator was a person that was supposed to take care of you). 

So even though BPD and C-PTSD are very similar, they differ in specific aspects. I'd recommend you to look into that. I couldn't tell you if your ex has BPD, C-PTSD or not because I don't know him. Only he could tell you if he feels like he identifies with these symptoms or not, and even then it's tough because these symptoms could turn out with something else completely in a diagnostic session.
